title: t02 Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO — narration (English)

items.title: On November 12th, 2026
items.subtitle: On November 12th, 2026, Nvidia filed a surprise notice with regulators.

items.title: Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company
items.subtitle: Jensen Huang, who co-founded the company, was out as CEO and as a director, effective immediately.

items.title: He'd run Nvidia for 33 years
items.subtitle: He'd run Nvidia for 33 years, and the filing didn't say why he was leaving.

items.title: The stock opened down
items.subtitle: The stock opened down more than ten percent, and still closed down more than four.

items.title: Four days before the filing
items.subtitle: Four days before the filing, he'd written to all his staff. One line read: "I was unfaithful to my wife."

items.title: He didn't say with whom.
items.subtitle: He didn't say with whom. It looked like a private matter.

items.title: And yet within days, Nvidia's board
items.subtitle: And yet within days, Nvidia's board, the US Congress, and China's Foreign Ministry were all weighing in.

items.title: So here's our take:
items.subtitle: So here's our take: the US-China tech war turned one CEO's private life into a national security issue.

items.title: That's not the same as saying
items.subtitle: That's not the same as saying he quit over national security. The company still hasn't said why he left.

items.title: Before we go on
items.subtitle: Before we go on, let's separate what's confirmed from what's only been reported.

items.title: Here's what's on the record.
items.subtitle: Here's what's on the record. Huang admitted, in writing, that he was unfaithful.

items.title: Nvidia's board opened an investigation
items.subtitle: Nvidia's board opened an investigation, citing reports that foreign intelligence had targeted him.

items.title: But the board also said it had no
items.subtitle: But the board also said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised.

items.title: And then he resigned
items.subtitle: And then he resigned, with no reason given.

items.title: Now, two more claims.
items.subtitle: Now, two more claims. Both are New York Times reports citing anonymous sources, and neither is confirmed.

items.title: One says US intelligence suspected
items.subtitle: One says US intelligence suspected a businesswoman close to him of spying for China.

items.title: She's a former executive
items.subtitle: She's a former executive at a Singapore company, and that company is an Nvidia customer.

items.title: The other says he'd had another relationship
items.subtitle: The other says he'd had another relationship, with an executive who reported to him. Nvidia declined to comment.

items.title: Now, the other side.
items.subtitle: Now, the other side. China's Foreign Ministry calls the "Chinese spy" claims groundless smears.

items.title: Singapore's Ministry of Home
items.subtitle: Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs says it never investigated the businesswoman for espionage.

items.title: Singapore police did
items.subtitle: Singapore police did look into her personally, though, over suspected false declarations when the company bought servers.

items.title: This February, they said there wasn't
items.subtitle: This February, they said there wasn't enough evidence against her. And no one has been charged.

items.title: So was the affair in his letter
items.subtitle: So was the affair in his letter with the businesswoman? He didn't say, and we don't know.

items.title: Either way, here's the real puzzle:
items.subtitle: Either way, here's the real puzzle: why would someone close to a CEO set off this many alarms?

items.title: Because Nvidia sells AI chips
items.subtitle: Because Nvidia sells AI chips, and whether the best ones can go to China is the front line of the tech war.

items.title: Nvidia's own annual report
items.subtitle: Nvidia's own annual report admits it's basically shut out of China's data center market.

items.title: And what Washington fears most is chips
items.subtitle: And what Washington fears most is chips slipping into China through Southeast Asia.

items.title: That's where the Singapore
items.subtitle: That's where the Singapore company comes in. The evidence against her fell short, but police are still investigating the company itself.

items.title: US export control officials
items.subtitle: US export control officials have inspected it too. The company denies any wrongdoing, and there's no conclusion yet.

items.title: So you've got the top chips
items.subtitle: So you've got the top chips, a customer suspected of rerouting them, and someone close to the CEO.

items.title: Put those three together
items.subtitle: Put those three together, and a private matter ends up under a national security magnifying glass.

items.title: Now look at how everyone responded.
items.subtitle: Now look at how everyone responded. They all pointed to the same thing.

items.title: The board cited reports that foreign
items.subtitle: The board cited reports that foreign intelligence had targeted him.

items.title: Three Republican committee chairmen
items.subtitle: Three Republican committee chairmen asked him for a closed-door briefing, on national security grounds.

items.title: On the day he resigned
items.subtitle: On the day he resigned, the head of the House China committee said Nvidia needs leaders who put national security first.

items.title: And that chairman urged Congress
items.subtitle: And that chairman urged Congress to move fast on export control laws.

items.title: Even China's Foreign
items.subtitle: Even China's Foreign Ministry made it about tech, telling the US to stop fabricating a "spy narrative" to justify a tech blockade.

items.title: So for all the shouting
items.subtitle: So for all the shouting, both sides agree on one thing: this is about chips.

items.title: Now, inside Washington.
items.subtitle: Now, inside Washington. On chip sales to China, lawmakers in both parties want to tighten, while the White House keeps loosening.

items.title: And Huang was on the White House's side
items.subtitle: And Huang was on the White House's side, so when the scandal hit, both parties used it to demand answers.

items.title: Take the tightening side first.
items.subtitle: Take the tightening side first. In October 2025, the Senate voted 77 to 20 for a provision limiting chip sales to China.

items.title: Then in March 2026
items.subtitle: Then in March 2026, one senator from each party jointly asked the Commerce Department to review Nvidia's export licenses.

items.title: Trump went the other way.
items.subtitle: Trump went the other way. In August 2025, he said he'd clear a chip for China if Nvidia would "pay us as a country something."

items.title: And after the scandal broke
items.subtitle: And after the scandal broke, he called Huang "a very honorable man."

items.title: Democrats went after Trump
items.subtitle: Democrats went after Trump, asking whether officials were told not to investigate because of Trump's ties to Huang.

items.title: Republicans went after the Commerce
items.subtitle: Republicans went after the Commerce Department and pushed export control bills.

items.title: But don't draw that line too neatly.
items.subtitle: But don't draw that line too neatly. Senator Warren, a Democrat, is also backing a Republican's bill to tighten exports.

items.title: The one clean difference is this:
items.subtitle: The one clean difference is this: Democrats name Trump. Republicans don't.

items.title: Speaking of the two parties
items.subtitle: Speaking of the two parties, there's a popular take in Chinese commentary: that Huang was a casualty of America's partisan fight.

items.title: Hong Kong outlet HK01 says Hu Xijin
items.subtitle: Hong Kong outlet HK01 says Hu Xijin, a well-known Chinese commentator, first claimed Democrats and the Washington establishment were targeting Huang to get at Trump.

items.title: A day later, he changed his tune:
items.subtitle: A day later, he changed his tune: Huang was a political casualty of vicious two-party fighting.

items.title: So first he blamed the Democrats
items.subtitle: So first he blamed the Democrats, then both parties.

items.title: So we checked.
items.subtitle: So we checked. Before he resigned, the only lawmaker we found publicly calling for him to go was Republican Senator Kevin Cramer.

items.title: And Trump, a Republican president
items.subtitle: And Trump, a Republican president, backed him the whole way.

items.title: The top House Democrat did say
items.subtitle: The top House Democrat did say resigning "was the right thing to do," but only after he'd already resigned.

items.title: There's no record of either
items.subtitle: There's no record of either party pushing him out.

items.title: Besides, the board had plenty
items.subtitle: Besides, the board had plenty of reasons of its own: his admission, the report of another relationship, and a shareholder lawsuit.

items.title: We'd say no one sacrificed him on purpose.
items.subtitle: We'd say no one sacrificed him on purpose. He did get caught in other people's fight, but nothing shows that's why he left.

items.title: Not everyone buys this.
items.subtitle: Not everyone buys this. The strongest pushback says national security is just noise, and he left over plain corporate governance.

items.title: He admitted infidelity
items.subtitle: He admitted infidelity, then a relationship with a subordinate was reported, and the board accepted his resignation that very day.

items.title: Any CEO could be gone over that. In 2018
items.subtitle: Any CEO could be gone over that. In 2018, Intel's CEO resigned over a relationship with an employee that broke company policy.

items.title: We agree with all of that
items.subtitle: We agree with all of that, and we never said he left over national security. The direct cause may well be governance.

items.title: But we're asking a different question:
items.subtitle: But we're asking a different question: how does one CEO's affair end up in front of Congress and China's Foreign Ministry?

items.title: Intel's case never did.
items.subtitle: Intel's case never did. And we think the difference isn't what he did. It's what his company sells.

items.title: Even if the spy reports
items.subtitle: Even if the spy reports turn out to be false, everyone's already treating this as a national security issue.

items.title: When the headlines fade, remember this:
items.subtitle: When the headlines fade, remember this: the more critical a company's product, the less private its leader's life gets.

items.title: Where his private life
items.subtitle: Where his private life ends isn't up to him. What his company sells decides it.

items.title: Coming up on November 17th
items.subtitle: Coming up on November 17th, Nvidia reports its first earnings without Jensen Huang.

items.title: There's no date yet for him
items.subtitle: There's no date yet for him to go before Congress, and none of the investigations has wrapped up.

items.title: That's where things stand
items.subtitle: That's where things stand as of November 14th. None of this is investment advice, and we'll keep following the story.
